title: When the variance is estimated
objectives: Use a $t$ test for a mean and compare it with the $z$ test.

screens.title: When σ is a guess
screens.prose: We rarely know $\sigma$. So we plug in the sample sd $s$ and form $t = \bar x/(s/\sqrt n)$. The table shows three funds with no skill, 8 months each, true $\sigma = 5\%$. The last column uses the true $\sigma$.
screens.question: For a fund with no skill, how often will luck give $|t| > 1.96$?

options.why: That holds when $\sigma$ is known. Here $s$ is random too: fund A’s came out small, and its $t$ jumped past 1.96.
An estimated $s$ adds noise. Extra noise spreads $t$ out; it does not pull it in.

options.text: It depends on the fund’s true mean
options.why: Under $H_0$ the true mean is fixed at 0. The answer depends only on $n$.

hints.text: Compare fund A’s $t$ with its $z$. What made them differ?
Fund A’s $s$ is far below the true 5%.
When $s$ is too small by luck, $t$ is too large. So large $|t|$ turns up more often than large $|z|$.

feedback.correct: More than 5%: a small $s$ by luck inflates $t$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at fund A: what did a small $s$ do to its $t$?

explain.text: Fund A’s $s$ came out at 2.75% instead of 5%, so its $t$ is 2.67 while its $z$ is 1.47. With 8 months, $|t| > 1.96$ happens 9.1% of the time, not 5%. The next screen shows the curve $t$ really follows.

screens.title: Heavier tails
screens.prose: Under $H_0$, $t$ follows the **$t$ distribution**, drawn in blue; the dashed curve is $N(0, 1)$. Its shape depends on the **degrees of freedom**, $n - 1$. The shaded tail is beyond 1.96.
screens.question: Set the degrees of freedom to 9, as for $n = 10$. What is the tail chance beyond 1.96?

hints.text: Slide the degrees of freedom to 9 and read the label above the tail.
The label gives $P(T \ge 1.96)$ for the current curve.
At 9 degrees of freedom the label reads 0.0408.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the slider to 9 and read the tail label.

byKey.normal: That is the normal tail. The $t$ tail beyond 1.96 is fatter.
byKey.two: That is both tails. The question asks for the shaded upper tail.
byKey.df10: That is 10 degrees of freedom. For $n = 10$ there are $n - 1 = 9$.

explain.text: With 9 degrees of freedom the tail beyond 1.96 is 0.0408, against 0.025 for the normal. Both tails hold 0.082, not 0.05. Slide up to 30 and the two curves almost meet.

screens.title: The t statistic
screens.prose: The statistic you formed is the **$t$ statistic**. Under $H_0$ it follows the $t$ distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom: $$t = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}.$$ A fund’s 10 months average $\bar x = 1.2\%$, with sample sd $s = 1.5\%$.

state.caption: The null curve: $t$ with 9 degrees of freedom

screens.question: What is $t$ for $H_0: \mu = 0$? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: The standard error is now $s/\sqrt n$.
The curve uses $n - 1 = 9$, but the standard error uses $\sqrt n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\bar x - \mu_0$ by $s/\sqrt n$, with $n = 10$.

byKey.s: You divided by $s$, the noise of one month. Divide by the standard error $s/\sqrt{10}$.
byKey.root-df: You divided by $s/\sqrt 9$. The degrees of freedom pick the curve; the standard error still uses $\sqrt n = \sqrt{10}$.
byKey.over-n: You divided by $s/n$. The standard error divides by $\sqrt n$.

explain.text: The standard error is $1.5/\sqrt{10} \approx 0.474\%$, so $t \approx 2.530$. We judge it against the $t$ curve with 9 degrees of freedom. Its tail beyond 2.530 is 0.016.

screens.title: The 9-df cut-off
screens.prose: A two-sided test at 5% puts 0.025 in each tail. With 9 degrees of freedom, 1.96 leaves too much in the tail. Find the right cut-off $c$.
screens.question: Slide the cut-off $c$ until the upper tail is 0.025.

hints.text: Watch the label: stop when it reads close to 0.025.
The label is the tail beyond your cut-off.
The tail is 0.0251 at 2.26 and 0.0247 at 2.27.

feedback.correct: About 2.262: the cut-off for 9 degrees of freedom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stop where the tail label reads 0.025.

byKey.normal: 1.96 leaves 0.041 in the $t$ tail. Move the cut-off further out.
byKey.far: You went too far: the tail is now well under 0.025.

explain.text: With 9 degrees of freedom the 5% two-sided cut-off is 2.262, not 1.96. The 10-month fund’s $t = 2.530$ clears it, so we reject $H_0$ at 5%. Its two-sided p-value is 0.032.

screens.title: Two observations
screens.prose: With only $n = 2$ months there is $n - 1 = 1$ degree of freedom. Two numbers give one difference, so $s$ is very unreliable.
screens.question: With 1 degree of freedom, how often does luck give $|t| > 1.96$?

hints.text: The label gives one tail. How many tails does $|t| > 1.96$ count?
The upper tail alone holds 0.1502.

feedback.correct: About 0.30: the tails are very heavy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Double the upper-tail label.

byKey.one-tail: That is the upper tail. $|t| > 1.96$ counts the lower tail too.
byKey.normal: That is the normal answer. With 1 degree of freedom the tails are far heavier.

explain.text: With 1 degree of freedom, $|t| > 1.96$ happens 30% of the time. The 5% cut-off is 12.706. Two months of data can hardly reject anything.

screens.title: Cut-offs shrink with n
screens.prose: Every $n$ has its own two-sided 5% cut-off. A strategy shows $t = 2.1$.
screens.question: For which record lengths does $t = 2.1$ reject $H_0$ at 5%?

options.why: You used the normal cut-off for every row. With $s$, small samples need larger cut-offs.
2.1 also clears 2.045, the cut-off for $n = 30$.
2.262 is the cut-off for $n = 10$ only. Larger samples have smaller cut-offs.

hints.text: Compare 2.1 with each row’s cut-off.
2.1 sits between the $n = 10$ and $n = 30$ cut-offs.
2.1 is above 2.045 and 1.984, but below 2.262.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check 2.1 against each cut-off in turn.

explain.text: 2.1 clears 2.045 and 1.984, but not 2.262. With $n = 30$ its two-sided p-value is 0.045; with $n = 10$ it is 0.065. As $n$ grows the cut-offs fall towards 1.96.

screens.title: Borrowing 1.96
screens.prose: An analyst has 8 months: $\bar x = 1.0\%$ and $s = 1.3\%$. She computes $t = 1.0/(1.3/\sqrt 8) = 2.176$. She compares it with 1.96 and rejects $H_0: \mu = 0$.

state.caption: $t$ with 7 degrees of freedom, and $N(0, 1)$ dashed

screens.question: What should she conclude at 5%, two-sided?

options.text: Fail to reject: with 7 degrees of freedom the cut-off is 2.365

options.why: You used the normal cut-off. With $s$ in place of $\sigma$ and $n = 8$, the cut-off is 2.365.

options.text: Fail to reject: with 8 degrees of freedom the cut-off is 2.306
options.why: Right decision, wrong degrees of freedom. They are $n - 1 = 7$.
That is one tail. The test is two-sided, so $p = 2 \times 0.033 = 0.066$.

hints.text: Which curve does $t$ follow when $\sigma$ is estimated from 8 months?
The shaded tail is one side only: 0.033.
Degrees of freedom $= 8 - 1 = 7$; the 5% cut-off is 2.365, above 2.176.

feedback.correct: 2.176 is below 2.365, so do not reject.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the $t$ curve with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.

byKey.normal: You used the normal cut-off. With $s$ in place of $\sigma$ and $n = 8$, the cut-off is 2.365.
byKey.df8: Right decision, wrong degrees of freedom. They are $n - 1 = 7$.

explain.text: With 7 degrees of freedom the two-sided p-value is $2 \times 0.033 = 0.066$, above 0.05. The normal curve would give 0.030 and a false sense of evidence. Small samples need the $t$ cut-off.

screens.title: z or t
screens.prose: With $\sigma$ known, $z = (\bar x - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ is $N(0, 1)$. With $\sigma$ estimated by $s$, $$t = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt n} \sim t_{n-1},$$ which has heavier tails and larger cut-offs. As $n$ grows, $s$ settles on $\sigma$ and $t_{n-1}$ approaches $N(0, 1)$.
screens.question: A desk knows its slippage sd is 6 bp from years of data. It tests 144 new orders. Which test fits?

options.text: A $t$ test with 143 degrees of freedom, to be safe
options.why: You used $t$ with $\sigma$ known. The $t$ curve pays for noise in $s$; with $\sigma$ known there is none to pay for.

options.text: A $t$ test with 144 degrees of freedom
options.why: You counted $n$ degrees of freedom, not $n - 1$. And with $\sigma$ known, $z$ applies anyway.

options.text: Neither: 144 orders are too many to test
options.why: A large sample is no obstacle. It makes the test sharper.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether $\sigma$ is known or estimated.

screens.title: A 12-month track record
screens.prose: A manager’s 12 monthly returns have mean 0.9% and sample sd 2.5%. Complete `t_test`, which returns $t$ and the two-sided p-value. `stats.t.sf(x, df)` is the upper tail $P(T \ge x)$ with `df` degrees of freedom.
screens.question: Complete `t_test(mean, sd, n, mu0=0.0)`.

widget.starter:
from scipy import stats
import math

def t_test(mean, sd, n, mu0=0.0):
    t = ...
    p = ...  # two-sided, df = n - 1
    return t, p
widget.solution:
from scipy import stats
import math

def t_test(mean, sd, n, mu0=0.0):
    t = (mean - mu0) / (sd / math.sqrt(n))
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), n - 1)  # two-sided, df = n - 1
    return t, p
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, each converted to float, rounded to 6 decimal places and compared with `math.isclose`. The first run loads SciPy, which is slow: allow up to a minute before the results appear.

hints.text: $t$ divides $\bar x - \mu_0$ by $s/\sqrt n$.
Two-sided: double the upper tail beyond $|t|$, with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.
Write `t = (mean - mu0) / (sd / math.sqrt(n))` and `p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), n - 1)`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the degrees of freedom, $n - 1$, and use `abs(t)` for the two tails.

byKey.test-1: For the manager the answer is $t = 1.2471$. Divide by `sd / math.sqrt(n)`.
byKey.test-6: A negative mean must give the same two-sided p-value. Use `abs(t)`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with an expression.

explain.text: The manager’s record gives $t = 0.9/(2.5/\sqrt{12}) = 1.247$ and $p = 0.238$ with 11 degrees of freedom. So we fail to reject $H_0$: a year of this record is well within luck. The normal curve would give $p = 0.212$, a little too small.

screens.title: A Sharpe ratio is a t statistic
screens.prose: A Sharpe ratio is mean return over sd. So $t = \bar x/(s/\sqrt T)$ is the Sharpe ratio times $\sqrt T$, for $T$ periods. The manager’s monthly Sharpe of $0.9/2.5 = 0.36$ gives $0.36\sqrt{12} = 1.247$, as before. You met this in skill versus luck.
screens.question: A fund reports an annualised Sharpe ratio of 0.8 over 5 years. About what is its $t$ statistic?

hints.text: With annual data, $T$ counts years.
The manager’s row shows the pattern: Sharpe times $\sqrt T$.
$0.8 \times \sqrt 5 \approx 0.8 \times 2.236$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the Sharpe ratio by $\sqrt T$, with $T = 5$.

byKey.times-t: You multiplied by $T$. Evidence grows with $\sqrt T$, as the standard error shrinks.
byKey.over-root: You divided by $\sqrt T$. More years give more evidence, so multiply.
byKey.sr: That is the Sharpe ratio itself. Multiply it by $\sqrt 5$.

explain.text: $t = 0.8\sqrt 5 \approx 1.79$, below the cut-off of about 2. Five years at a Sharpe ratio of 0.8 is not yet clear evidence of skill. Reaching $t = 2$ needs $T = (2/0.8)^2 = 6.25$ years.

ideas: With $\sigma$ unknown, use $t = (\bar x - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt n)$. Under $H_0$ it follows the $t$ distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.
The $t$ curve has heavier tails, so its 5% cut-offs are larger: 2.262 for $n = 10$, 2.045 for $n = 30$, 1.984 for $n = 100$.
As $n$ grows, $t_{n-1}$ approaches $N(0, 1)$. A Sharpe ratio’s $t$ statistic is the Sharpe ratio times $\sqrt T$.

formula.name: The t statistic
formula.note: Use it when $\sigma$ is estimated by $s$; with $\sigma$ known, use $z$.

summary.trap: 1.96 belongs to a known $\sigma$. With $s$ and a small sample, use the $t$ cut-off for $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.

quiz.prose: A $t$ test uses 15 monthly returns and their sample sd.
quiz.question: How many degrees of freedom does its $t$ distribution have?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The degrees of freedom are $n - 1$.

byKey.n: You used $n$. Estimating the mean uses up one, leaving $n - 1$.
byKey.two: You took away 2. A one-sample test loses only one, for the mean.

explain.text: The sample sd measures spread about $\bar x$, which was itself estimated. That uses up one degree of freedom, leaving $15 - 1 = 14$.

quiz.prose: Returns $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are independent and normal with mean $\mu_0$ under $H_0$. $s$ is their sample sd.
quiz.question: Which statistic follows the $t$ distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom?

options.why: You used the true $\sigma$. That statistic is exactly $N(0, 1)$.
You left out $\sqrt n$. That divides by the noise of one return, not of the average.
You put $n - 1$ under the root. The degrees of freedom name the curve; the standard error keeps $\sqrt n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The $t$ statistic replaces $\sigma$ by $s$ in the $z$ statistic.

explain.text: Replacing $\sigma$ by $s$ in $z$ gives $t = (\bar X - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt n)$. The extra randomness in $s$ fattens the tails into $t_{n-1}$. With $\sigma$ itself the statistic stays $N(0, 1)$.

quiz.prose: A strategy’s 25 monthly returns have mean 0.4% and sample sd 1.0%. The two-sided 5% cut-off with 24 degrees of freedom is 2.064.
quiz.question: What does the $t$ test of $H_0: \mu = 0$ conclude at 5%?

options.why: You used the normal cut-off. With $s$ estimated from 25 months, the cut-off is 2.064.
You divided by $s$, not by $s/\sqrt{25} = 0.2$. Then $t$ is 2.0.
You divided by $s/n$. The standard error is $s/\sqrt n = 0.2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $t = 0.4/(1.0/\sqrt{25})$, then compare it with 2.064.

explain.text: The standard error is $1.0/5 = 0.2$, so $t = 2.0$. That is below the 24-df cut-off of 2.064, so we fail to reject. Against 1.96 it would have been called significant.

quiz.prose: With $n = 400$, the two-sided 5% cut-off for $t$ is 1.966.
quiz.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: For large $n$, the $t$ and $z$ tests nearly agree
The $t$ test should never be used for large $n$
options.why: It can be used; it simply gives almost the same answer as $z$.

options.text: The $t$ test is now stricter than with small $n$
options.why: It is looser: 1.966 is far below small-sample cut-offs such as 2.262.
$s$ settles close to $\sigma$, but it is never exactly equal. The cut-off is still a little above 1.96.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 1.966 with the normal cut-off.

explain.text: With 399 degrees of freedom, $s$ is a precise estimate of $\sigma$. So $t_{399}$ is almost $N(0, 1)$, and its cut-off 1.966 is almost 1.96.
